props.title: Ruhr

sections.content: James Benning's **Ruhr** (2009) represents a masterclass in observational cinema, following his signature style of fixed-frame long takes but marking his first digital work. Like his earlier **13 Lakes** (2004) and **Ten Skies** (2004), Benning employs extreme duration to force viewers to deeply contemplate industrial and natural landscapes. The film's six segments examining Germany's Ruhr Valley industrial region build on themes explored in structural films like Michael Snow's **Wavelength** (1967) and Hollis Frampton's **Zorns Lemma** (1970).

sections.content: The film's most discussed segment - a 60-minute static shot of a coke processing tower releasing steam - recalls Andy Warhol's **Empire** (1964) in its meditation on duration and industrial processes. But where Warhol's 8-hour static shot of the Empire State Building aimed to bore viewers into new perceptions, Benning's precisely timed industrial releases create a hypnotic rhythm that transforms the mechanical into the sublime. This approach influenced later observational works like Wang Bing's **West of the Tracks** (2002) and Nikolaus Geyrhalter's **Homo Sapiens** (2016).

**Ruhr** marked a pivotal moment in slow cinema, bridging analog and digital techniques while maintaining the genre's core focus on duration, landscape and industrial spaces. Its influence can be seen in works like Sharon Lockhart's **Double Tide** (2009) and Denis Côté's **Bestiaire** (2012), which similarly use fixed frames and extended duration to examine labor and environment. sections.content: The shift to digital marked by **Ruhr** (2009) opened new possibilities for duration in experimental film. While maintaining Benning's characteristic precision, digital allowed for longer takes without film reel changes, as demonstrated in later works like **BNSF** (2013) and **natural history** (2014). This technical evolution parallels similar transitions in works like James Benning's **Twenty Cigarettes** (2011) and Kevin Jerome Everson's **Park Lanes** (2015).
